_note: Ranking the World's Most Polite Languages, recounted 2026-10-24 with the expanded database in polite_research/ (English Wiktionary for ~100 languages, 16 native Wiktionaries, JMdict, CC-CEDICT, Poedjosoedarmo's Javanese word list; one rule set, duplicates and expressions removed, see polite_research/README.md). Tibetan (52, would be #8) has no recording of a polite word on Commons, so it is skipped and Polish (#11, 44) takes #10. Vietnamese fell to 18.
title: Ranking the World's Most Polite Languages
subtitle: BY THE NUMBER OF POLITE WORDS IN THE DICTIONARIES
outro: Which language is the most polite?

items.name: Chinese
cards: Chinese has a polite 'you': 您 (nín) instead of 你 (nǐ). And to ask a stranger's name, you ask for their 'precious surname'.
The humble side counts too: traditionally your own home is 'my cold hut' (寒舍) and your own work 'my clumsy work' (拙作).

items.name: Japanese
cards: Japanese politeness has three layers: polite words, honorific words that raise others, and humble words that lower yourself.
Even 'to be' changes: iru with friends, irassharu for someone you respect, and oru for yourself when being humble.

items.name: Javanese
cards: Javanese has separate vocabularies by social level: ngoko for friends, krama for elders and strangers, krama inggil for the deepest respect.
Even colours change: red is 'abang' to a friend but 'abrit' to your elders. A scholarly list of these polite words has over 900 of them.

items.name: Korean
cards: Korean grammar has up to seven speech levels, built into the end of every verb. This greeting uses the most formal one.
Even eating changes: 먹다 (meokda) for yourself, 드시다 (deusida) for your elders. That politeness lives in grammar, so a word count underrates Korean.

items.name: Thai
cards: Thai ends polite sentences with a little word that depends on who is talking: 'khrap' if you are a man, 'kha' if you are a woman.
Thai has a whole royal vocabulary, rachasap: special words used only for the king and the royal family. Most of its count comes from them.

items.name: Burmese
cards: Mingalaba comes from 'mingala', a blessing. The 'pa' at the end is a politeness particle that softens almost any Burmese sentence.
Burmese speakers put a respectful title before almost every name: U for an older man, Daw for an older woman, Ko for a young man.

items.name: English
cards: English lost its polite 'you'. 'Thou' was the friendly one and 'you' the polite one, until everyone became 'you'.
English is polite with phrases, not special words: 'could you possibly…', 'would you mind…'. 'Please' itself is short for 'if it please you'.

items.name: Indonesian
cards: 'Terima kasih', thank you, literally means 'receive affection': you thank someone by accepting what they gave.
Indonesians use family titles with everyone: Bapak (father) for any older man, Ibu (mother) for any older woman, even in shops and offices.

items.name: Malay
cards: Malay has a royal vocabulary too: a king does not eat (makan) but 'santap', does not sleep (tidur) but 'beradu', and does not die (mati) but 'mangkat'.
Even the everyday polite 'I', saya, comes from 'sahaya', an old word for servant.

items.name: Polish
cards: Polish has no polite 'you' pronoun. To a stranger you say Pan (sir) or Pani (madam) and talk to them in the third person: 'Does the lady want coffee?'
And 'proszę' does almost everything: please, here you go, you're welcome, and 'pardon?' when you didn't hear.
